title: Why the Moon looks so big when it rises
description: Sometimes the rising Moon looks ENORMOUS — like a giant coin rolling up behind the houses. But it is a trick your eyes and brain play together. The Moon does not really grow.

body.heading: The giant Moon trick
paragraphs: On some evenings, the full Moon rises looking huge — much bigger than the small Moon you see high in the sky later that night. It feels impossible, but the Moon is exactly the same size all night long. It does not swell, and it does not come closer while you watch.
It is a trick called the Moon illusion. Your brain is the trickster — and it is tricking you to be helpful, not naughty.

body.heading: How to catch the trick
paragraphs: When the Moon hangs low near trees and rooftops, your brain compares it with those things and decides: that must be enormous. High in the empty sky there is nothing to compare it with, so your brain calls it small. Same Moon, different neighbours.

You can catch the trick yourself. Hold your thumb up at arm's length next to the giant rising Moon — your thumbnail covers it! Do the same when the Moon is high and small. Your thumb covers it exactly the same. The Moon never changed. Your brain did.

takeaway: The rising Moon only looks giant: your brain compares it with trees and houses and guesses wrong — your thumbnail covers it just the same, high or low.
materials: A clear evening when the Moon is rising (optional)
supervision: A grown-up reads with the child and joins any evening Moon watching from a safe spot at home.
safetyNotes: Moon watching happens at home or in the garden with a grown-up, never out alone after dark.
Never look at the Sun — this trick is only for the Moon.
screenFreeExtension: Draw the Moon twice: once big behind the houses, once small and high — then draw your thumb next to both to show the trick.
